hints: Think about whether you can efficiently test a proposed value for the maximum allowed distance.
For a gap of length gap and a proposed distance d, determine how many equal-sized pieces are required and therefore how many new stations are needed.
The feasibility of d is monotone, so binary-search d between 0 and the largest original gap.
title: Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station Problem

notes: For a candidate maximum distance d, each original gap of length gap requires ceil(gap / d) - 1 additional stations.
Binary search the smallest feasible d over the range from 0 to the largest original gap.
Floating-point answers are accepted within 10^-6 of the correct value.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [[stations], K]

sampleTestCases.explanation: There are nine unit gaps and nine additional stations. Put one new station in each gap, so every gap becomes 0.5.
The final gap has length 11. With one additional station it is split into two gaps of length 5.5, while the other gaps have length 1, so the maximum is 5.5.
The final gap has length 92. One additional station splits it into two gaps of length 46, while all earlier gaps have length 1, so the optimum is 46.

content.problemStatement:
On a horizontal number line, we have gas stations at positions `stations[0], stations[1], ..., stations[n-1]`, where `stations[i] < stations[i+1]`. Now, we add `K` more gas stations so that the maximum distance between adjacent gas stations is minimized. Return the smallest possible value of the maximum distance between adjacent gas stations.

Your answer will be accepted if it is within `10^-6` of the correct answer.

**Constraints:**

* `10 <= stations.length <= 2000`
* `0 <= stations[i] <= 10^8`
* `stations[i] < stations[i+1]`
* `1 <= K <= 10^6`

notes: The search interval is [0, max adjacent gap].
The feasibility check is monotone: if d is feasible, every larger distance is also feasible.
The implementation performs 100 binary-search iterations, which is sufficient for the required 1e-6 accuracy under the stated coordinate bounds.
solution.approach: Binary-search the answer. For a candidate maximum adjacent distance d, a gap of length gap requires ceil(gap / d) - 1 new stations. Sum that requirement over all adjacent gaps; if it is at most k, d is feasible. Binary search the smallest feasible d.

better.complexity: O((n + k) log n) time and O(n) space.
better.description: Use a max-heap that repeatedly places a new station into the gap whose current largest sub-gap is greatest. This gives a useful constructive approach and improves over enumerating all distributions, but its dependence on k is too large for the upper constraint.

optimal.complexity: O(n log(D / epsilon)) time and O(1) auxiliary space, where D is the largest original gap.
optimal.description: Binary-search the minimum possible maximum distance. For each candidate d, compute how many new stations are needed in every original gap using ceil(gap / d) - 1. Because feasibility is monotone, binary search finds the optimum to the required precision.

bruteForce.complexity: O(C(k+n-2, n-1) * n) time in a distribution-enumeration formulation, with O(n) auxiliary space.
bruteForce.description: Try distributing the k new stations among the original gaps and evaluate the resulting maximum gap. Enumerating all distributions is combinatorial and becomes infeasible quickly.

solution.timeComplexity: O(n log(D / epsilon)), where n is stations.length, D is the largest original gap, and epsilon is the required precision.

followUps: Why does the feasibility check become monotone as the candidate distance increases?
How would a max-heap solution compare with binary search when k is small?
How would you change the approach if the required precision were 1e-9?

learningObjectives: Recognize when an optimization problem can be solved by binary-searching the answer.
Derive a monotone feasibility check from the number of stations required in each gap.
Reason about floating-point precision and stopping criteria in numerical binary search.
